title: Smart Energy Monitoring
summary: A project direction exploring how embedded measurement might make electrical energy data easier to understand.
objective: Explore how embedded measurement and electrical energy data can be combined in a documented monitoring system.
problem: This is a project track, not a built device. The intended question is how useful electrical measurements can be collected and presented in a responsible, understandable way.
approach: No hardware architecture, component selection, firmware, or test plan is being claimed yet. Those details will be added only after they are actually designed and reviewed.
results_note: No prototype, simulation, repository, or measured results are published for this concept.

case_study.overview: A design brief for an energy-monitoring system, written before any hardware exists. It fixes the problem, the requirements and the open engineering choices, so the eventual schematic and firmware can be judged against something rather than invented after the fact.
case_study.application: The intended application is low-voltage, supervised measurement of an appliance or small installation: enough to answer “what is this load actually drawing, and when?” without claiming revenue-grade accuracy or mains-connected deployment.

requirements.text: Measure voltage and current of a single low-voltage DC load at a useful rate (at least tens of samples per second) and derive power.
Keep measurement uncertainty stated, with a calibration procedure against a reference meter.
Record or display data locally so a network outage does not lose the measurement.
Stay inside a supervised, low-voltage boundary; any mains-referenced variant requires isolation review before it is attempted.
Publish the architecture, calibration method and test conditions alongside any number, so a reader can check the claim.

sensing_options.note: Best linearity and low-side simplicity; adds a small series drop and needs attention to common-mode range if used high-side.
Isolated by construction, simpler to wire, but offset drift and temperature behaviour need checking against the datasheet.
Cheap and predictable, but the divider loads the node and its impedance must suit the ADC sample-and-hold.
Fewer analog decisions to make, less of the signal chain to learn — a trade of effort against understanding.

case_study.architecture_label: Proposed functional roles · no component has been selected

architecture.name: Electrical input
architecture.detail: A low-voltage measurement boundary; source, range and isolation approach are still open.

architecture.name: Signal path
architecture.detail: A proposed conditioning and sampling stage; gain, filtering and reference are undecided.

architecture.name: Embedded processing
architecture.detail: A candidate role for RMS and power computation; firmware is not written.

architecture.name: Data use
architecture.detail: Possible logging or display direction; interface and connectivity are undecided.

mcu_options.note: Wi-Fi and a capable ADC on one part; ADC linearity needs care and calibration.
Better analog peripherals and deterministic timing; connectivity needs additional design.
Moves accuracy requirements into a component with a proper datasheet, at the cost of board complexity.

case_study.isolation: The first study stays low-voltage and supervised. A mains-referenced version would need galvanic isolation, creepage and clearance decisions, protective devices and review by someone qualified to sign it off — that is out of scope for this record.
validation: Compare against a calibrated reference meter at several operating points and record the deviation.
State ambient temperature, instrument, wiring and load for every measurement.
Repeat measurements over time to separate drift from noise.
Publish failed checks as well as passing ones.

roadmap.deliverable: This design brief and the open-questions list.
Ranges, accuracy target and safety boundary written down and reviewed.
Block diagram with chosen sensing method and interfaces.
Signal-chain model covering divider loading, gain and quantization.
Schematic, PCB revision and firmware repository.
Bench comparison against a reference meter with conditions recorded.

open_questions: Which measurable quantity and operating range should the first study address?
Shunt, Hall-effect, or integrated monitor — which trade-off is worth learning first?
How is the ADC reference stabilised so the measurement means something?
What information would make the output useful without implying more accuracy than the measurement supports?
future_directions: Publish the requirements table once the operating range is chosen.
Compare candidate sensing approaches from datasheets and a signal-chain model.
Only publish a schematic, simulation or firmware when those artifacts exist.
